chapter_theme: The woman wastes away in grief through the night, caught between a love she can't hide and a shame that forbids telling him. Love is measured against the sea and against the night, and the only company that remains is the night itself.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar sees them mostly as answers to her friend: on concealment and messages (1161-1163), rafts (1164), a rebuke to the friend (1165), the balance of pleasure and pain (1166), and the night (1167-1169). He says 1170 prepares for the next chapter on the eyes.

1161.reading: The woman says she would hide this pain, but, as water does in a spring when one draws from it, it only rises.
1161.nuance: The commentators differ quietly over what the drawing out is. Kalaignar makes concealing itself the action, so hiding is what increases it. For Parimelazhagar, the concealment simply fails, as water wells up for one who draws from a spring.

1162.reading: The woman says she cannot hide this sickness, and telling the one who caused it also brings her shame.
1162.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a remarkable reason for the shame: if she sends a messenger, it will imply she is still alive. The grief that is meant to prove love would be disproved by being reported. Her friend has offered her two options, and she refuses both.

1163.reading: The woman says love and shame hang from the ends of a carrying pole, which is her life, within her body that can't bear it.
1163.nuance: The verb தூங்கும் conveys the balance: as Parimelazhagar reads it, neither side outweighs the other, so she can't commit to either, and the pole will snap. Kalaignar shifts the image so that the body is the pole; the verse says the life is.

1164.reading: The woman says the sea of love certainly exists, and the safe raft for crossing it certainly doesn't.
1164.nuance: Parimelazhagar takes the missing raft as a reproach to the friend, who should have sent word and been the raft. Manakkudavar agrees that she means she has no helper. It is more personal than a cosmic complaint.

1165.reading: The woman asks what those who can bring such grief in friendship would do in enmity.

positions.position: It is a rebuke to the friend, for not sending a messenger when she could have prevented the grief.
positions.quote: தூது விடாமை நோக்கித் தோழியோடு புலந்து சொல்லியது

positions.position: It is about the lover, who gives her the grief of parting even while they are close.

1166.reading: The woman says the pleasure of love is a sea, and when love afflicts her, the pain is greater than the sea.
1166.nuance: This rejects a consoling arithmetic. The friend has said that those who've had the joy should expect the pain, and the woman's point, as Parimelazhagar glosses it, is that an equal measure could be borne, but this isn't equal.

1167.reading: The woman says she swims the fierce flood of love and sees no shore, and even at midnight there is only herself.
1167.nuance: யானே உளேன் can mean 'I alone am here', and for Parimelazhagar also 'I am still alive', which he attributes to some evil deed's result. That idea of past deeds is his and isn't in the verse. Pope's prose follows him by adding 'still I live'.

1168.reading: The woman says the night, which puts all living beings to sleep, is to be pitied, as it has no companion but her.
1168.nuance: Everything turns on அளித்து. It is usually a word of pity or grace, and Parimelazhagar marks it as contempt: the night has foolishly chosen as its companion someone about to die. She isn't lamenting her solitude so much as mocking her only companion.

1169.reading: The woman says these long nights passing now are crueller than the cruelty of that cruel man.
1169.nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses the implicit contrast: nights that were short when they were happy have now grown long. The word கொடியார், 'the cruel one', replaces his name.

1170.reading: The woman says that if her eyes could go where he is as her heart does, they wouldn't be swimming in a flood of tears.
1170.nuance: For Parimelazhagar, the mind's journey is only thought, while eyes need a body to walk there, so what the heart can do isn't really a substitute for seeing. He says this verse opens the next chapter, and the eyes' complaint begins here.

links.note: Both use water that rises as you draw it. In 396, the well is knowledge, and more study brings more. In 1161, the well is pain, and every attempt to bail it out adds more. The image of an inexhaustible resource is the same, and it is a blessing in one and a curse in the other.

The man sets shame aside to mount the palmyra horse (1132). The woman carries shame and love in perfect balance and can drop neither (1163). The book states this asymmetry directly: he can choose and she can only bear the weight.
The man's flood simply takes his raft. The same phrase, காமக் கடும்புனல், in the woman's verse has her still swimming at midnight with no shore. The image remains and the endurance lengthens.

source_issues: 1162: Kalaignar's entry ends with stray text, எ. சுருக்க விளக்கம் சுருக்க விளக்கத்துக்கு, which is not commentary on this verse. It was not used.
1169: The verse text in the source has a stray leading '>' character.
1170: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It begins at நீந்தல மன்னோவென் கண் with no headnote or complete gloss.
